newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada pipeline race to produce winners and losers.
newsitem.headline: Canada pipeline race to produce winners and losers.

text.p: An unprecedented spate of proposals aimed at boosting Canadian natural gas exports to the United States is raising new questions over just how much capacity is too much and which pipelines will get built.
Planned and proposed pipeline projects aimed at moving more Canadian gas to the U.S. Midwest and Northeast by the turn of the century are now valued at more than $10 billion (C$13.8 billion).

Taken together, proposals on the drawing board represent an increase in Canadian export capacity of more than 8.5 billion cubic feet per day, about three-quarters of the gas produced each day in the province of Alberta's gas basin.

"There's no way in the world that all the projects that have been announced lately will go in the time frame that the project developers are talking about," said Roland George, vice-president of the Canadian Energy Research Institute.
"There would be just too much pipe capacity coming on too quickly, and if you put all that capacity in, you start to ask whether the basin can support that."

Over the past month, billions of dollars worth of new pipelines and expansions have been announced by such firms as Coastal Corp., Northern States Power Co., Columbia Gas System Inc., Westcoast Energy Inc. and CMS Energy Corp.
New projects include the Viking Voyageur Gas Transmission line to the U.S. Midwest from Emerson, Manitoba, and the Great Lakes Gas Transmission expansion and Millenium Pipeline to the Northeast.

These, which would all be in service by the year 2000, are on top of the Northern Border Partners LP 700 million cubic feet per day expansion and extension to Chicago slated to be in service by the end of 1998.

The New England region is also set for over 480 million cubic feet per day of gas that would flow from the proposed Sable Island gas project offshore Nova Scotia as well as 178 million cubic feet per day from the planned Portland Natural Gas Transmission system.

The dominant company in the race, and the key firm in nearly all the proposals, is TransCanada PipeLines Ltd., which operates Canada's 7 billion cubic feet a day mainline. It would transport gas to all the just-announced pipelines and has a stake in most of them.

TransCanada, which will add 289 million cubic feet of capacity this year, could boost its total by 1.4 billion cubic feet per day by the turn of the century under its so-called Nexus staged expansion programme which will ship the new gas to Emerson, Manitoba.

The Canadian Energy Research Institute forecasts show Canada's total gas output is expected to rise to about 7 trillion cubic feet annually by the year 2010, including export volumes of 3.7 trillion cubic feet.
That's an increase from total output of 5.41 trillion cubic feet in 1996, with 2.8 trillion cubic feet being shipped to the United States for about 13 percent of U.S. demand.

While gas demand in the United States is expected to grow by 1 percent to 2 percent a year over the next decade, Canada's market share is projected to stay in the 12 percent to 14 percent range, George said.
Ron Barrone, a New York-based pipeline analyst with PaineWebber, said the United States has the ability to absorb all the gas Canada can send, but not without dire consequences on U.S. prices.

Today's hot pipeline activity contrasts sharply with just two years ago, when Canadian gas producers, hammered by far lower prices than those in the United States, were criticising pipeline companies for not providing enough export space to meet growing production.

Canadian producers and analysts have long said that, without more takeaway capacity from Alberta, Canada's biggest producing province, gas was being trapped within its borders and competition to sell it was driving prices down.
Industry officials say the trigger for today's explosion of competing proposals was the development of the producer-backed Alliance Pipeline project.

Alliance, a consortium of 18 companies including Alberta Energy Co. Ltd., Gulf Canada Resources Ltd., Chevron Corp., Canada Resources and IPL Energy Inc., aims to ship 1.3 billion cubic feet of gas a day to Chicago from northeast British Columbia, a 3,000 km (1,864 mile) route.
The project, with an estimated cost of C$3.6 billion ($2.6 billion), would be in service by late 1999. It is currently before regulators in Canada and the United States.
